_comment: EXP-74. Same three workloads, same SLO block, same transcript as m1; ONLY the
request-count ratio differs. Written 2026-08-10.
WHY. The hour-trace advantage over llm-d is +24.3 points on the per-request
denominator, and decomposing it by class on the EXP-71 runs gives +26.1 from
chat, -0.7 from deep research and -1.1 from swe: the whole of it is the chat
term, and it is that large because chat is 78.1% of requests. The mix MOVING is
backed by Azure data (conv/code ratio 12.0% -> 56.7% over the day); the mix
LEVEL 10:2:1 is a number this project chose and has never varied on the
post-2026-08-08 workload. m2 (40:2:1) and m3 (6:1:2) exist but keep chat at 93%
and 67% of requests and were measured on the pre-fix workload.
These two take chat out of the majority: m4 puts it at 57% of requests and m5 at
33%. Nothing else changes -- same slo block, same mean_input_tokens, same swe
transcript, same 10,000-conversation chat pool -- so the difference between a
run on m1 and a run on these is the composition and nothing else.
WHAT MOVES WITH THE RATIO, and why no profile regeneration is needed. The
scheduler's class profile (deploy/profiling/.../fluidserve.json) holds per-class
OUTPUT LENGTH distributions, which do not depend on how many of each class
arrive. Arrival composition is measured online by both FluidServe and the
PolyServe repartitioner. So the CLAUDE.md rule 'changing the workload means
changing the profile too' does not bite here -- it bites when a class's output
length distribution changes, which is what happened when deep research went from
282 to 985 tokens.
Mean tokens per request implied by each ratio (from mean_input_tokens above and
the measured output means chat 428 / dr 985 / swe 520):
so the saturating arrival rate is expected to fall roughly in proportion to the
output mean. That expectation is what the two scouting rates bracket.
This file: m4 -- chat 57.1% / deepresearch 28.6% / swe 14.3% of requests. m1 SLO block.
